hook: Leave a glass of water on a sunny windowsill and another in a cool cupboard. A week later the windowsill glass is lower. Was it the warmth? The light? The draft from the window? Unless you change one thing at a time, you cannot tell, and every lab question on the exam starts by asking which thing you changed.

prereq.q: To escape from liquid water as vapor, what must a water molecule do?
options: Break the hydrogen bonds holding it to its neighbors
Break the covalent bonds inside the molecule
Gain extra hydrogen atoms from the air
prereq.why: Evaporation means pulling free of neighboring molecules, which are held by hydrogen bonds. The covalent bonds inside the molecule stay intact.

prereq.q: A student measures 30, 32, 31 and 45 drops. Which summary is least affected by the 45?
prereq.why: The median depends only on the middle of the sorted values, so one extreme value barely moves it.

figure.caption: A controlled experiment on evaporation: change one factor (temperature), measure one result (mass lost), and keep everything else the same.

chain.cause: You ask a testable question: does temperature affect how much water evaporates in 24 hours?
chain.effect: The question names the factor you will change (temperature) and the result you will measure (mass lost).
Temperature is the independent variable: you choose its values.

chain.cause: You weigh each dish before and after 24 hours.
chain.effect: Mass lost is the dependent variable: it may respond to temperature.

chain.cause: You keep dish shape, starting mass, time and air movement identical in every group.
chain.effect: These controlled variables cannot explain a difference, so a change in mass lost can be traced to temperature.

chain.cause: You run three dishes per temperature and add an unheated group for comparison.
chain.effect: Repeats show chance variation, and the control group shows the baseline, so you can judge whether temperature really made a difference.

ideas: Worked example. "Dishes of 50.0 g water at 20, 30 and 40 °C; mass lost in 24 h measured." Independent variable: temperature (set). Dependent variable: mass lost (measured). Controlled: dish, starting mass, time, air movement. Control group: unheated dishes. If-then: if temperature rises, then more water evaporates, because more molecules escape their hydrogen bonds.
Quick test: the independent variable is what you set before the run; the dependent variable is what you read off at the end.
A control group is a whole group given the baseline; a controlled variable is one factor held the same in every group. Exams mark answers down for mixing them up.
If two factors change together (temperature and a fan), the result cannot be traced to either one. Look for that flaw in every described experiment.

misconception.wrong: The control group is the group where everything is controlled.
misconception.right: Every group in a good experiment has the same controlled variables. The control group is the one given the baseline condition (no treatment, or the normal value), used for comparison.

summary: A controlled experiment changes one factor, the independent variable, and measures one response, the dependent variable. Everything else is held constant as controlled variables, a control group shows the baseline, and repeated runs show chance variation. A testable question names both variables, and an if-then prediction links them with a reason.
